list.listitem: Consider enuresis in any child who was dry and begins wetting or who urinates into clothes or bed at least twice a week for 3 months after 5 years of age. C
Use history and physical to exclude associated symptoms and conditions including lower urinary tract symptoms, sleep apnea, ADHD, and developmental or neurologic problems. C

In secondary enuresis, consider underlying medical conditions such as diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, urinary tract infection, or psychological stressors such as parental separation or abuse. C
Simple behavioral approaches (e.g., reward charts, timed voiding, avoiding caffeine, and avoiding fluids before bedtime) are recommended as initial therapy as they are safe and may be helpful. A
Consider alarm treatment with or without desmopressin when simple behavioral interventions fail. A

background.definition: Enuresis is the inappropriate discharge of urine past the age of usual control. Nocturnal enuresis is enuresis at night; diurnal enuresis includes daytime wetting. Children with primary enuresis have never had an extended period of dryness. Children with secondary enuresis have new wetting symptoms after they have stayed dry for at least 6 months. Monosymptomatic enuresis is nocturnal enuresis without any daytime lower urinary tract symptoms. Polysymptomatic or non-monosymptomatic enuresis includes those with other lower urinary tract symptoms.

list.listitem: Nocturnal enuresis more common in boys (3-1)
Intermittent bedwetting occurs in 30% of children age 4 to 5 years, and 9.5% of those at age 9 years.

Nocturnal enuresis: (defined as frequency of twice per week for at least 3 consecutive months or the presence of clinically significant distress or impairment) occurs in 6.2% of boys and 2.5% of girls age 8 to 11 years.
The emotional and social impact on the child can be significant and the clinician should be sensitive to these issues.
Enuresis may create conflict in the home and result in isolation or exclusion from sleepovers, campouts, and so forth.
Genetic pattern: loci on chromosomes 12, 13, and 22 have been identified.

The risk of enuresis in a child is increased if both parents had enuresis (77%), or if one parent had the diagnosis (44%). The risk is also increased with comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), sleep apnea, or habitual snoring (22%-27%).
Sleep arousal disorders.
Bladder issues, decreased bladder capacity, or detrusor overactivity.
Nocturnal polyuria relative to nocturnal bladder capacity.
Central etiology suggested by associated conditions: ADHD, sleep apnea, and habitual snoring.
Constipation frequently associated symptom.
Several mechanisms are proposed, but the definitive pathophysiology is unknown.
Bladder issues: hyperactive detrusor activity or lack of inhibition, decreased bladder capacity.
Reduced arousability: sleep studies show minimal increased delta waves and REM sleep.

Nocturnal polyuria from altered circadian rhythm of desmopressin has been proposed. However recent studies suggest that other physiological responses to vasopressin are responsible and unrelated to urine output.
Studies on children with habitual snoring and sleep apnea have demonstrated increased levels of B-type natriuretic peptide, which may inhibit vasopressin.

Suspected defect in the Locus Coeruleus in the upper Pons suggested as underlying lesion due to its function in sleep arousal, anatomically related to the pontine micturinic center and has axonal connections to the hypothalamic release of vasopressin.

list.listitem: DSM-V criteria for enuresis include:
Repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes (whether involuntary or intentional).

The behavior is clinically significant as manifested by either a frequency of twice a week for at least 3 consecutive months or the presence of clinically significant distress or impairment in social, academic (occupational), or other important areas of functioning.
Chronological age is at least 5 years (or equivalent developmental level).

The behavior is not due exclusively to the direct physiological effect of a substance (e.g., a diuretic, anti-psychotic, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or a general medical condition (e.g., diabetes, spina bifida, or seizure disorder).
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.

Ask about symptoms of urinary tract infection (frequency, urgency, hesitation, dysuria, fever), sleep apnea (loud snoring, apnea), ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, tic disorders, obsessive compulsive disorder, anxiety, developmental or neurologic problems, and drinking habits.
Ask about stooling habits as constipation may be a contributing cause.
Ask about medication use, including diuretics, anti-psychotics, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Symptoms of non-monosymptomatic enuresis (overactive bladder): leaking urine during the day (drops of urine in underpants before/after voiding, very wet underpants, continuous leakage, daytime incontinence), urination 8 or more times per day, sudden/urgent need to urinate.

Symptoms of dysfunctional voiding: voiding postponement (urination 3 or fewer times per day), holding urine (e.g., Vincent's curtsy—pressing heel into perineum, crossing legs, standing on tiptoes), need to push in order to urinate, interrupted urinary stream or several voids one right after another.

In secondary enuresis, consider underlying medical conditions such as diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, urinary tract infection (UTI), or psychological stressors such as parental separation or abuse.
A 2-week voiding diary to assess nighttime urine production and daytime bladder capacity may be helpful.

The physical examination should focus on the genitourinary tract (phimosis, labial agglutination, examination of underwear). Also assess for neuromuscular disease through lower extremity musculoskeletal and neurological examination including lumbosacral spine, weight/height. Consider rectal exam.
Obtain a urinalysis to exclude secondary causes, may not be necessary if monosymptomatic.
Consider urodynamic testing if patient has polysymptomatic enuresis or for treatment failures.
Consider obtaining urine specific gravity on first morning urine to predict treatment responses to desmopressin acetate.
Evaluation of a child with enuresis seeks to differentiate those with primary enuresis and secondary enuresis, monosymptomatic and polysymptomatic enuresis, and those with comorbidities.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation, and for a suggested approach to therapy.
Simple behavioral approaches (e.g., reward charts, timed voiding, avoiding caffeine, and avoiding fluids before bedtime) are recommended as initial therapy as they are safe and may be helpful. A
Consider alarm treatment when simple behavioral interventions fail. A
Timed voiding may be effective in children with diurnal enuresis. C
Desmopressin is effective, especially for children with polysymptomatic enuresis, but has a high relapse rate when discontinued. A
See for a suggested approach to therapy.

Desmopressin (10-40 mcg nasal spray or 200-600 mcg tablets): up to 80% of patients have a good or partial response. The onset of response is quicker than with alarm therapy, but therapies are equally effective at 3 months, with a higher relapse rate when desmopressin is stopped than with alarm therapy. The number needed to treat for 14 consecutive dry nights is 14. There is a risk of hyponatremia, so counsel against high fluid intake and larger than recommended dose. Trials indicate that the oral and nasal routes are equally effective. The initial treatment trial should be for 3 to 6 months; you may continue for up to 1 year. For nasal route, begin at 10 mcg and titrate by 10 mcg until dryness is achieved. For oral route, begin at 200 mcg and increase weekly to 600 mcg by 100 to 200 mcg increments. Consider a trial of tapering the medication every 3 months.

Combining desmopressin with alarm therapy likely reduces the number of wet nights at the end of treatment (MD -0.88, 95% CI -1.38 to -0.38) and increases the number of patients achieving 14 consecutive dry nights at end of treatment (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.51).
Antispasmodics may be more effective when combined with desmopressin and were well tolerated, faster, and more cost effective than single drug therapy in one study.

Tricyclic antidepressants produce a reduction of 1 wet night per week while the patient takes the medication, but come with a high relapse rate and potentially serious adverse effects of overdose. Imipramine was better than some antidepressants, but not significantly different from other tricyclics, and combination with oxybutynin was more effective than monotherapy with lower relapse rate. Bedwetting alarms were more efficacious both short- and long-term than tricyclic antidepressants. Nortriptyline and mianserin were no more effective than placebo.

A small study of children with refractory primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis suggested that fluoxetine may be more effective than placebo in achieving a partial (66.1% vs 16.7%, p<0.01, NNT=2) or complete (7.1% vs 0%, p<0.01, NNT=14) response within 4 weeks of initiating therapy.
Indomethacin and diclofenac were better than placebo but not as good as desmopressin and include a greater risk of adverse effects.

A small RCT with 21 children with urinary incontinence and occult tethered cord syndrome were randomized to usual care or surgery (surgical section of the filum). After 8 years, outcomes were nearly identical between groups.

A secondary analysis was performed of a randomized trial designed to compare adenotonsillectomy with watchful waiting in children with non-severe obstructive sleep apnea. At baseline about 30% in each group reported "bedwetting" in a parental survey. Seven months post-operatively, enuresis was twice as likely to have resolved (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 3.1) in the surgery group.

A Cochrane review found weak evidence to support the use of hypnosis, psychotherapy, acupuncture, chiropractic adjustments, and medicinal herbs to treat nocturnal enuresis, but only with single small trials. There is weak evidence that hypnosis is better than imipramine (1 trial).
There is also weak evidence that acupuncture and chiropractic adjustments were better than sham treatments.
Homeopathy treatments were better than placebo but not as successful as desmopressin.

Simple behavioral interventions may be effective for some, and are recommended as first-line treatments because alarms and drugs are more demanding and may have adverse effects. Interventions should include star charts/reward systems, demystifying the problem, waking the child to urinate during the night.
Timed urination may be useful in those with diurnal enuresis (daytime wetting).

Alarm treatments are effective and are recommended for patients not responding to simple behavioral techniques. Alarm treatments have a low relapse rate. A combination with medications does not consistently increase effectiveness.

Alarm training with overtraining or "dry bed training" (which involves waking routines, positive practice, cleanliness training, and bladder training) may be slightly more effective than alarm alone, with slightly lower relapse rates.
A systematic review of wearable alarm systems for daytime urinary incontinence found no significant benefit (RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.8 to 2.6).
A retrospective study found no difference between family assistance with awakening and relying on the child to wake him or herself.
Increasing the bladder capacity does not appear to be useful in treating enuresis.

In children with overactive bladder, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) was better than sham therapy in resolution of daytime incontinence (64% vs 0%) with 10 minutes of stimulation 3x/week, but 11% of patients had enuresis recur after discontinuing therapy.
A small study of parasacral TENS in single weekly sessions found that it provided some benefits over sham TENS.

A systematic review identified 4 RCTs with 208 children comparing parasacral TENS with sham or usual care. There was no difference in response rates between groups. None of the secondary analysis found any benefit to parasacral TENS.
In a study of children 5 to 17 years with bladder and bowel dysfunction, TENS improved functional constipation but not bladder symptoms.
A review concluded that more well designed RCTs are needed of nerve stimulation modalities.
Consider referral to urology for abnormal voiding behaviors, straining, or unusual posture.
Consider referral to urology for polysymptomatic enuresis if there is no response to drug therapy.
A total of 15% of cases will naturally resolve each year. Less than 1% to 3% persist into teen years or young adulthood; most of these are polysymptomatic. A
Frequent (every 3 weeks) follow up during behavioral and alarm approaches may increase the likelihood of response. C
The maximum effectiveness of most treatments occurs at 3 months, so follow-up in 3 months is appropriate. C
Understand that enuresis is a nonvolitional problem and almost all cases will resolve with time.
Encourage adequate daytime fluids and avoid excessive fluids prior to bedtime
Encourage the child to take responsibility for his or her own care, including washing clothing. Avoid punishment.
Treat comorbidities such as constipation, daytime urinary symptoms, and sleep apnea prior to addressing nocturnal symptoms.
Parental assistance to help the child get to the toilet to finish voiding is a key factor in the success of alarm therapy.

Consider treatments for primary monosymptomatic enuresis ()
Polysymptomatic enuresis: Consider treatments for symptoms, timed voiding, oxybutinin, etc. Consider referral if ineffective or if unusual posturing
Psychological stressors/symptoms (ie, recent family changes, divorce, suggestion of abuse)?
Physiological symptoms (ie, fevers, dysuria, polyphagia, polydipsia, weight changes)?

Educate and reassure patient and family of nonvolitional nature of problem, inform them of the natural history and that there is no underlying physiological or psychological issue (demystify the problem)
Treat co morbidities such as constipation, sleep apnea and daytime urinary symptoms

Behavioral approach: (1) Maintain good daytime hydration, limit fluids before bedtime, especially caffeine; (2) encourage using bathroom before bedtime; (3) use reward chart for dry nights; (4) involve child in caring for laundry/cleanup without being punitive; (5) try waking child and taking to bathroom during the night; (6) keep voiding log book
Alarm therapy. Important that both child and parents are motivated
Desmopressin: 10-40 micrograms nasally or 200-400 micrograms tablet orally, titrate weekly to effective dose
Continue desmopressin. Add oxybutynin 2.5 mg to 5 mg orally up to TID
